design_detail: Double-blind, placebo-controlled, within-person laboratory study at the National Institute of Mental Health in 15 healthy volunteers recruited through the NIH normal volunteer programme. Each person had two test days, one with ketamine and one with saline, in randomized order and at least one day apart, after an overnight fast. On each day an intravenous bolus of 0.12 mg/kg was followed immediately by an infusion of 0.65 mg/kg over 1 hour (a total of 0.77 mg/kg over the hour; the infusion was capped at 58 mg), or by matching saline. Cognitive testing (a one-list task giving an attention score, free recall and recognition memory of categorically related words) was done 30 minutes before the infusion and at 10, 55, 90 and 120 minutes after it started; the 18-item Brief Psychiatric Rating Scale (BPRS) was rated at 55 and 90 minutes. The infusion ran for the first 60 minutes, so the 10- and 55-minute tests were during it and the 90- and 120-minute tests after it. The pre-specified questions were whether the memory effects were independent of the effect on attention (tested by analysis of covariance with the attention score as covariate) and whether they were related to the psychosis ratings (tested by correlating the ketamine-minus-placebo changes at 55 minutes). No plasma concentrations were measured; no physiological or mood measures are reported.
can_establish: Whether a single 1-hour intravenous ketamine infusion, compared with saline in the same people, lowers scores on one attention measure, free recall and recognition memory of a 12-word categorical list and raises BPRS symptom ratings during and shortly after the infusion in 15 healthy volunteers, and whether the memory effects at the 55-minute time point survive adjustment for the attention score measured at the same time.
cannot_establish: That the memory effects are unrelated to the psychosis ratings (the correlations are null in 14 to 15 people, which is far too few to show independence); the mechanism of the memory effect (the design cannot separate acquisition, consolidation and retrieval, and the authors' acquisition-versus-retrieval argument rests on comparing two tasks of unequal difficulty); any effect after 120 minutes, after repeated use, by other routes, or in people who are not screened healthy volunteers; and any relation to blood levels, which were not measured.

sample.recruitment: Recruited through the National Institutes of Health normal volunteer programme (p. 302).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Free of psychiatric disorders by the Schedule for Affective Disorders and Schizophrenia (SADS) structured interview, and in good health by physical examination, electrocardiogram and laboratory tests including liver and thyroid function tests and urinalysis (p. 302). No further inclusion or exclusion criteria are stated: no age range, no exclusion of substance use or of previous experience of ketamine or phencyclidine, and no drug-screening or abstinence requirement is described.
sample.demographics: 15 people: 12 men and 3 women, mean age 27.9 (SD 7.1). No other demographic information is reported: ethnicity, education, weight, previous drug experience and smoking are all absent (p. 302).
sample.attrition: All 15 completed both test days. One person did not complete recognition-memory testing at the 55-minute time point on the ketamine day, and that person's recognition data were excluded altogether, leaving 14 for recognition memory (p. 302). No reason is given for the missed test.
sample.selection_effects: A small, mostly male sample of volunteers screened for psychiatric disorder and medical illness at a research institute. Because the paper reports no screening for drug use and no previous drug experience, it is not known whether any participant had used ketamine or a related drug before, which matters both for tolerance and for how recognizable the condition was.

exposure.measurement: Drug given by the investigators; no plasma ketamine or norketamine concentrations were measured and no assay is described. Drug screening of participants is not mentioned.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions only, as the investigators gave them: on one test day an intravenous bolus of ketamine 0.12 mg/kg followed by an infusion of 0.65 mg/kg over 1 hour, that is 0.77 mg/kg over the hour, with the infusion limited to a maximum of 58 mg; on the other test day saline. Order randomized, test days at least one day apart, both after a fast from midnight, with bilateral antecubital intravenous lines placed 60 minutes before dosing (p. 302). Whether the doses are of the hydrochloride salt or of the base is not stated.
exposure.polysubstance: Not reported: no drug-use history, no urine screen and no restriction on alcohol, tobacco or caffeine is described anywhere in the paper.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Only a fast from midnight before each study day is stated (p. 302); no drug or alcohol abstinence period and no verification are described.

comparison.controls: Each participant's own saline day (within-person placebo), with the order of the two days randomized and at least one day between them.
comparison.matching: Within-person comparison. No period or carryover analysis is reported, and because the same task structure was used on both days with different word lists, practice effects across the two days are possible but are not examined.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable to a within-person comparison; a baseline measurement 30 minutes before each infusion serves as that day's reference.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Not applicable (the same people served as their own controls).

outcomes.instruments: One word-list procedure yielded all three cognitive measures (p. 302). A list of 12 categorically related words (typical members of categories such as vegetables, fruit and animals) was read at one word every 2 seconds; 6 of the 12 were read once and 6 were repeated after at least two other words had intervened, and the participant had to say 'repeat' when a word recurred, which requires holding the words in working memory for up to 34 seconds. The number of repetitions correctly identified is the attention score. After an activity-filled 2-minute delay the participant recalled all the words freely (free recall). After a further 30-second activity-filled delay a new list of 24 words from the same categories was read, containing the 12 previous words and 12 distractors, and the participant judged each as old or new (recognition memory). The tasks are described as standardized and validated in studies of drug effects in patient populations. Behaviour: the 18-item Brief Psychiatric Rating Scale (BPRS), analysed as a total score and as the empirically derived factors thought disorder, withdrawal-retardation, anxiety-depression and hostility-suspiciousness, with individual items examined afterwards.
outcomes.validity_norms: The word-list tasks come from the group's own earlier drug studies; no norms, no reliability data and no parallel-form data for the lists used on the two days are given. The maximum scores are 6 for attention (6 repeated words), 12 for free recall and 24 for recognition; the paper reports recognition near 11 of what appear to be 12 scorable items on placebo (Figure 1), so the scoring of recognition is not fully specified. The BPRS is a standard instrument; the item scoring runs from 1, so a three-item factor has a floor of 3 and the 18-item total a floor of 18, which matters for reading the printed means.
outcomes.operationalization: 'Impairment' is a significantly lower score on the ketamine day than on the placebo day, by repeated-measures ANOVA with a Greenhouse-Geisser correction and post-hoc tests at individual time points; 'psychosis' is the BPRS total and its factors. All measures are acute: cognitive testing ran from 10 to 120 minutes after the infusion started and behavioural ratings at 55 and 90 minutes, with the infusion running for the first 60 minutes. The study was done entirely in healthy volunteers; no patients were studied and nothing was measured after 120 minutes.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None stated. Editors' count of the measures analysed: 3 cognitive measures, BPRS total and 4 factors, and 3 further analyses (the covariance analyses, the correlations and the item-level comparisons), with 5 individual BPRS items tested by t test and 7 correlations reported, all at an uncorrected threshold. The Greenhouse-Geisser correction addresses sphericity within an ANOVA, not multiplicity across measures.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: The test days are described as double-blind with saline as the comparison infusion (p. 302), but no masking procedure, no statement of who rated the BPRS, and no blinding check are given. The BPRS and the word-list tasks were administered by staff; the placebo-day BPRS scores show almost no variation (thought disorder 3.0, SD 0.0 at every time point, Table 1), so any rater who saw a nonzero score knew the day was not placebo. The authors themselves could not run the covariance analysis on the BPRS because of the lack of variance in the placebo condition (p. 303).

analysis.effect_sizes: Only F statistics, p values and figure plots; no means with SD or SEM for the cognitive measures (these appear only in Figure 1), no confidence intervals and no standardized effect sizes. Free recall: drug F1,14=9.63 (p=.008), time F4,56=5.16 (p=.005), drug x time F4,52=4.35 (p=.004); post hoc, lower on ketamine at 55 minutes F1,13=18.79 (p=.001) and at 90 minutes F1,13=6.25 (p=.026). Recognition memory: drug F1,13=17.48 (p=.001), time F4,52=6.05 (p=.001), drug x time F4,52=7.95 (p<.001); lower at 10 minutes F1,13=8.92 (p=.01) and 55 minutes F1,13=18.78 (p=.001). Attention: drug F1,14=9.63 (p=.008), time F4,56=5.37 (p=.003), drug x time F4,56=2.71 (p=.05); lower at 55 minutes F1,14=8.79 (p=.01). Editors' calculation of within-person standardized differences at 55 minutes from the printed F statistics (the square root of F divided by the square root of n): about 1.2 for free recall, 1.2 for recognition memory and 0.8 for attention. Editors' reading of Figure 1 (p. 303), whose values are not printed: at 55 minutes free recall falls from about 6.2 on placebo to about 3.2 on ketamine, recognition from about 11.3 to about 8.0, attention from about 5.4 to about 4.2. BPRS total 19.3 (SEM 0.4) at baseline, 27.5 (1.6) at 55 minutes and 21.5 (1.4) at 90 minutes on ketamine, against 19.1 (0.7), 18.7 (0.4) and 18.7 (0.3) on placebo (Table 1, p. 304).
analysis.covariates: The attention score at 55 minutes was used as a covariate in analyses of covariance of free recall and recognition memory; the drug x time interaction remained significant for free recall (F1,12=6.55) and recognition memory (F1,13=7.05, p=.025) (p. 304). Nothing else was adjusted for: age, sex, order of test days and period effects are not in any model. Analysis of covariance with the BPRS could not be done because the placebo-day scores had almost no variance (p. 303).
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol, registration or pre-specified primary outcome is mentioned; the hypotheses are stated in the introduction (that ketamine would impair memory and attention and that these effects would be independent of each other and unrelated to the psychotomimetic effects, p. 302), which is a statement of intent rather than a registered plan.
analysis.selective_reporting: The three cognitive measures and all four BPRS factors are reported, with null results for hostility-suspiciousness and for the anxiety-depression interaction, and the null correlations are reported in full and plotted. Against this: no table of cognitive means is given, so the size of each effect can be read only from a figure; the individual BPRS items reported are the significant ones plus hallucinations, with no statement of how many items were tested; and the proportions of individual participants who worsened are given for every measure, which is a form of presentation that favours the drug effect without adding a test.
analysis.power: Not reported; no sample-size calculation. The paper's central negative claim, that the memory effects are not related to the psychosis ratings, rests on correlations in 14 to 15 people. Editors' calculation: with n=15 the 95% interval around the reported r=-.28 runs from about -0.69 to 0.27, and the study has roughly 19% power to detect a true correlation of 0.3 at p=.05 two-sided; about 62 participants would be needed for 80% power at r=0.35. The null correlations therefore cannot establish independence.

interpretation_gap.results_show: In 15 healthy volunteers, a 1-hour intravenous ketamine infusion lowered free recall and recognition memory of a 12-word categorical list and lowered one attention score during the infusion, with the largest differences at 55 minutes and recovery by 90 to 120 minutes; it raised the BPRS total score by about 8 points at 55 minutes, almost entirely through the thought-disorder and withdrawal-retardation factors, with hallucination ratings not significantly raised. The memory effects at 55 minutes remained significant when the attention score at the same time point was used as a covariate. The correlations between the memory changes and the symptom changes were small and not significant, in a sample far too small to show their absence.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract states that the memory impairments were not accounted for by changes in attention and were not significantly related to psychosis ratings, and concludes that the NMDA receptor plays a direct role in two types of explicit memory (p. 301). 'Not significantly related' is accurate as a description of the test; the discussion turns it into a stronger claim, that ketamine has direct effects on free recall and recognition memory and that the attentional and behavioural disturbances were not related to the memory impairments (pp. 304-305), which null correlations in 14 to 15 people cannot support. The 'direct role in two types of explicit memory' also goes beyond a study with no measurement of any mechanism. The discussion further argues that ketamine preferentially impairs acquisition rather than retrieval, because both free recall and recognition fell; this inference assumes the two tasks are equally sensitive, which the paper does not show, and the authors' own description of recognition as the easier task makes the comparison uncertain. The abstract's claim that ketamine induced 'a brief psychosis' rests on a BPRS total of 27.5 against a placebo floor of 18 and on no significant increase in hallucination ratings, and the authors themselves note in the discussion that ketamine did not commonly induce hallucinations or paranoid delusions in their volunteers (p. 305).

timeline.event: A randomized saline-controlled study of 40-minute infusions in 18 healthy volunteers reported the same acute rise in BPRS positive and negative symptom scores and a fall in delayed word recall, with immediate three-word recall unchanged at ceiling

A four-condition steady-state infusion study in 15 healthy men with measured plasma concentrations reproduced the fall in verbal declarative memory and found it at and below the concentrations that produced other symptoms, while sustained attention, verbal fluency and spatial working memory were unaffected
An earlier study of subanaesthetic injections reported lower recall of a 24-item list (Ghoneim et al., 1985), cited by this paper as showing effects on immediate as well as delayed recall
A six-person study of ketamine and sensory perception reported acquisition deficits with retrieval relatively spared (Oye et al., 1992), on which this paper's acquisition argument partly rests

replication.where_it_stands: That a subanaesthetic ketamine infusion lowers verbal learning and memory scores acutely in healthy volunteers is well replicated, including in a steady-state design with measured plasma concentrations (Newcomer et al., 1999). The specific claims of this paper are weaker: that the memory effect is independent of attention rests on one covariance analysis at one time point, and that it is unrelated to the psychotomimetic effect rests on null correlations in 14 to 15 people. Whether ketamine's memory effect is primarily on acquisition remains unsettled.

funding.funder: Not reported: the paper carries no funding statement and no acknowledgments section. The work was done in the Experimental Therapeutics Branch of the National Institute of Mental Health and the Division of Intramural Clinical and Biological Research of the National Institute on Alcohol Abuse and Alcoholism, Bethesda, Maryland, so it is intramural US federal research, but no grant or support is named (pp. 301, 306).
funding.declared_conflicts: Not reported: the paper carries no conflict-of-interest statement, which was not usual practice in 1996.
funding.affiliations_note: All authors were at US National Institutes of Health intramural branches; no industry sponsor is named.

what_would_settle_it: A within-person study large enough for the independence question (on the order of 60 to 100 participants, or a design with several concentrations per person), with a described and tested blind, measured plasma concentrations, memory tasks matched for difficulty so that free recall and recognition can be compared, separate manipulation of encoding and retrieval (material learned before the infusion and retrieved during it, and the reverse), and mediation analysis rather than a null correlation, so that the attentional, symptom and memory effects can be told apart.

domains.domain: Randomization process (order of the two test days)
domains.note: The order of ketamine and placebo was randomized, but no sequence generation or allocation concealment is described, and no period or order effect is reported. Baseline scores on the two days look similar in Figure 1 and Table 1, which is reassuring.

Test days were separated by at least one day, which is ample for ketamine's elimination, so pharmacological carryover is unlikely. Practice on a repeated word-list procedure is a real concern: different lists were used but their equivalence is not demonstrated, and no period effect is reported.

Described as double-blind with a saline comparison, but no masking procedure and no blinding check are reported. The placebo-day BPRS scores are almost invariant (thought disorder 3.0 with SD 0.0 at all three time points, Table 1), so any rater seeing a raised score knew the condition; 13 of 15 participants had raised thought-disorder scores on the ketamine day. The key outcomes include clinician ratings.

All 15 completed both days. One person's recognition-memory data were dropped entirely because one time point was missed, so recognition rests on 14, and no reason for the missed test is given; the degrees of freedom shift between 13 and 14 across analyses without explanation.

All outcomes are rater-administered or rater-rated in a condition that was probably recognizable. The three cognitive measures come from one word-list procedure, so they are not independent of each other (the drug effects on free recall and recognition correlate at r=.64), and the attention measure used as a covariate is derived from the same list the memory scores come from, which makes the covariance analysis difficult to interpret.

No protocol or registration; no table of cognitive means, so effect sizes can only be read from a figure; item-level BPRS tests reported for the significant items plus hallucinations without stating how many were tested. Null results are reported in full, which is in the paper's favour.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: The within-person design with a saline day, randomized order and a baseline on each day makes the acute drug effects on the word-list measures and the BPRS internally credible, and they match what other laboratories have found. The overall judgment is set by the unverifiable blind in a study whose outcomes are all rater-administered, by the measurement problem that the attention covariate comes from the same task as the memory scores, and by the fact that the paper's distinctive claim is a negative one drawn from correlations in 14 to 15 people. The source can be cited for the acute size and time course of the fall in free recall, recognition memory and the attention score, and for the BPRS changes by factor and item, in 15 screened healthy volunteers given a 1-hour infusion; it cannot be cited for the independence of ketamine's memory effects from its attentional or psychotomimetic effects, for a preferential effect on acquisition, or for any statement about concentrations, which were not measured.

key_findings.finding: Free recall of a 12-word categorical list was lower on the ketamine day than on the placebo day in 15 healthy volunteers: drug F1,14=9.63 (p=.008), time F4,56=5.16 (p=.005), drug x time F4,52=4.35 (p=.004); post hoc, lower at 55 minutes F1,13=18.79 (p=.001) and at 90 minutes F1,13=6.25 (p=.026). Thirteen of the 15 showed a decrease in free recall from their own pre-infusion baseline at 55 minutes of the ketamine infusion.
key_findings.locator: Results, 1st paragraph (left column) continuing in the right column; Figure 1, middle panel
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation of the within-person standardized difference at 55 minutes: about 1.2 (square root of 18.79, divided by the square root of 14). Editors' reading of Figure 1 (middle panel), whose values are not printed: about 6.2 words on placebo against about 3.2 on ketamine at 55 minutes.

key_findings.finding: Recognition memory for the same words was also lower on the ketamine day (n=14): drug F1,13=17.48 (p=.001), time F4,52=6.05 (p=.001), drug x time F4,52=7.95 (p<.001); post hoc, lower at 10 minutes F1,13=8.92 (p=.01) and at 55 minutes F1,13=18.78 (p=.001). Nine of the 14 showed a decrease in recognition from their own pre-infusion baseline at 55 minutes of the ketamine infusion.
key_findings.locator: Results, 1st paragraph (right column); Figure 1, bottom panel
key_findings.note: Editors' reading of Figure 1 (bottom panel), whose values are not printed: about 11.3 on placebo against about 8.0 on ketamine at 55 minutes; by 90 minutes the two curves have met.

key_findings.finding: The attention score (correctly identifying the repeated words while the list was read) fell less markedly: drug F1,14=9.63 (p=.008), time F4,56=5.37 (p=.003), drug x time F4,56=2.71 (p=.05); post hoc, lower at 55 minutes only, F1,14=8.79 (p=.01). Nine of the 15 showed a decrease in attention from their own pre-infusion baseline at 55 minutes of the ketamine infusion.
key_findings.locator: Results, 1st paragraph (right column); Figure 1, top panel
key_findings.note: The attention measure comes from the same word list as the two memory measures, so the three scores are not independent. The paper prints the identical drug-effect statistic F1,14=9.63, p=.008 for both free recall and attention (see reporting issues). Editors' calculation: F4,56=2.71 gives p=.039 uncorrected against the printed .05, which is presumably after the Greenhouse-Geisser correction the methods name, so the attention effect is the least secure of the three.

key_findings.finding: The effects on free recall and recognition remained significant when the attention score at 55 minutes was used as a covariate: free recall F1,12=6.55 and recognition memory F1,13=7.05 (p=.025).
key_findings.locator: Results (continued), 3rd paragraph of the left column
key_findings.note: The printed p value for the free-recall analysis of covariance is 0.25, which does not match F1,12=6.55 (editors' calculation: p=.025) and is almost certainly a typographical error for .025 (see reporting issues). The covariate is derived from the same task as the outcome.

key_findings.finding: BPRS total score rose on the ketamine day from 19.3 (SEM 0.4) at baseline to 27.5 (1.6) at 55 minutes and 21.5 (1.4) at 90 minutes, against 19.1 (0.7), 18.7 (0.4) and 18.7 (0.3) on placebo; drug F1,82=24.20, time F2,82=9.00 and drug x time F2,81=10.37, all p<.001.
key_findings.locator: Results, last paragraph of the right column (p. 303); Table 1 (p. 304)
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation: the 18-item BPRS has a floor of 18, so the peak mean of 27.5 is 9.5 points above the floor and 8.2 above the same day's baseline. The degrees of freedom (1,82 and 2,81) do not correspond to 15 people measured at three time points (see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: Of the four BPRS factors, only thought disorder and withdrawal-retardation changed significantly. Thought disorder rose from 3.0 (SEM 0.0) to 6.3 (0.6) at 55 minutes and 3.5 (0.2) at 90 minutes on ketamine, against 3.0 (0.0) at all three time points on placebo (drug F1,82=39.65, time F2,82=25.30, drug x time F2,81=24.99, all p<.001). Withdrawal-retardation rose from 3.3 (0.1) to 6.6 (0.6) and 4.6 (0.5), against 3.3 (0.2), 3.5 (0.2) and 3.5 (0.2) on placebo (drug F1,82=21.58, time F2,82=11.21, p<.001; drug x time F2,81=8.12, p=.001). Anxiety-depression showed a drug effect only (F1,82=7.51, p=.007) with no time or interaction effect, and hostility-suspiciousness showed nothing (F=0.1, p=.90).
key_findings.locator: Results, last paragraph of the right column (p. 303) continuing on p. 304; Table 1 (p. 304)
key_findings.note: Each three-item factor has a floor of 3, so the peak thought-disorder score of 6.3 is 3.3 points above the floor. Thirteen of 15 had a rise in thought disorder, 14 of 15 in withdrawal-retardation, 6 of 15 in anxiety-depression and 1 of 15 in hostility-suspiciousness (p. 303).

key_findings.finding: At the 55-minute peak, the items driving the thought-disorder factor were conceptual disorganization (ketamine 2.9, SD 1.1, against placebo 1.0, SD 0.0; t=6.42, p<.001) and unusual thought content (2.2, SD 1.1 against 1.0, SD 0.0; t=4.29, p<.001). The hallucinations item did not differ significantly (1.2, SD 0.5 against 1.0, SD 0.0; t=1.38, p=0.190). In the withdrawal-retardation factor, emotional withdrawal (2.1, SD 0.9 against 1.2, SD 0.4; t=3.67, p=.003), motor retardation (2.3, SD 0.9 against 1.2, SD 0.4; t=5.91, p<.001) and blunted affect (2.2, SD 0.9 against 1.1, SD 0.3; t=4.94, p<.001) were all higher on ketamine.
key_findings.locator: Results (continued), last paragraph of p. 303 (right column) and 1st paragraph of p. 304 (left column)
key_findings.note: The paper does not say whether the spread printed with these item means is a standard deviation or a standard error; the SD label is the editors' reading, consistent with the printed t values for n=15 (for example (2.9-1.0)/(1.1/sqrt 15) = 6.7 against the printed 6.42). BPRS items are scored from 1, so a mean of 1.0 with no spread on placebo is the floor. The degrees of freedom of these t tests are not printed. Together with the unchanged hostility-suspiciousness factor (F=0.1, p=.90; 1 of 15 rose, key finding 5), the unchanged hallucinations item means that this study should not be cited for ketamine producing hallucinations or paranoid symptoms in these volunteers.

key_findings.finding: The ketamine-minus-placebo changes in memory at 55 minutes were not significantly correlated with the ketamine-minus-placebo changes in symptom ratings: free recall with BPRS total r=-.28 (p=.31), with thought disorder r=-.31 (p=.26), with withdrawal-retardation r=-.11 (p=.71); recognition memory with BPRS total r=-.28 (p=.34), with thought disorder r=-.41 (p=.14), with withdrawal-retardation r=.02 (p=.96). The two memory changes correlated with each other (r=.64, p=.01), and the changes in thought disorder and withdrawal-retardation did not (r=.06, p=.83).
key_findings.locator: Results (continued), 4th and 5th paragraphs of the left column; Figure 2 (four panels, right column)
key_findings.note: n=15 for the free-recall correlations and 14 for the recognition correlations. Editors' calculation: the 95% interval around r=-.28 with n=15 runs from about -0.69 to 0.27 and around r=-.41 with n=14 from about -0.77 to 0.15, so these results are compatible with moderate associations in either direction and cannot show independence.

key_findings.finding: The ketamine effects were short-lived: by the 90-minute cognitive test (30 minutes after the end of the infusion) recognition memory had returned to the placebo level and free recall was closing on it, and by 120 minutes all three measures overlapped; on the BPRS, thought disorder had fallen from 6.3 to 3.5 at 90 minutes (placebo floor 3.0).
key_findings.locator: Figure 1, all three panels (p. 303); Table 1, +90 Min. column (p. 304)
key_findings.note: Nothing was measured after 120 minutes, and no follow-up on later days is reported, so the card can say only that the measured effects had largely resolved by 2 hours.

reporting_issues.issue: The analysis of covariance for free recall is printed as F(1,12)=6.55, p=0.25, a p value that does not match the statistic and is not significant, in a sentence stating that the effect remained significant; the companion analysis is printed as F(1,13)=7.05, p=.025.
reporting_issues.consequence: Almost certainly a typographical error for p=.025 (editors' calculation from F1,12=6.55 gives p=.025), but as printed the paper's central adjustment result reads as non-significant. A claim resting on this analysis must note the discrepancy.

reporting_issues.issue: The degrees of freedom of the BPRS analyses (drug F1,82, time F2,82, drug x time F2,81) are far too large for 15 people rated at three time points; a within-person analysis of 15 people at three time points gives error degrees of freedom of about 14 and 28. The t tests on individual BPRS items are printed without degrees of freedom.
reporting_issues.consequence: The BPRS tests appear to treat observations rather than people as the unit of analysis, which would make the p values much smaller than they should be. The direction and size of the BPRS changes (Table 1) can be cited; their significance levels cannot be checked.

reporting_issues.issue: The same statistic, F(1,14)=9.63, p=.008, is printed as the drug effect for free recall and, in the next paragraph, as the drug effect for attention.
reporting_issues.consequence: One of the two is probably a transcription error; a reader cannot tell which measure the value belongs to, and the two effects should not be quoted as independently equal.

reporting_issues.issue: The degrees of freedom shift between analyses of the same measure without explanation: free recall has drug F1,14 and time F4,56 (implying 15 people) but a drug x time interaction of F4,52 and post-hoc tests of F1,13 (implying 14); the attention analyses use F4,56 and F1,14 throughout. Only the recognition-memory exclusion of one participant is explained.
reporting_issues.consequence: The number of people behind each free-recall statistic is uncertain, so the sample size attached to the free-recall result should be given as 14 to 15.

reporting_issues.issue: No table or text gives the means and standard deviations of the three cognitive measures; they appear only as plotted points with error bars in Figure 1.
reporting_issues.consequence: Effect sizes can be computed only from the F statistics or read approximately from the figure; the encyclopedia should cite the test statistics, and any magnitude read from Figure 1 must be labelled as read from a figure.

reporting_issues.issue: The paper reports no drug-use history, no urine screening, no abstinence requirement and no previous-exposure information for the participants, and gives no age range, weight or ethnicity beyond a mean age and the sex split.
reporting_issues.consequence: It cannot be established whether any participant had used ketamine or related drugs before, which bears on tolerance and on how recognizable the ketamine day was; the sample cannot be compared with those of other laboratory studies.

reporting_issues.issue: The recognition-memory scale is not fully specified: the task has 24 items (12 old, 12 distractors), but the plotted placebo scores sit at about 11 and the axis runs to 12, so either only the 12 old items or some other subset was scored.
reporting_issues.consequence: The maximum score of the recognition measure is unknown, so a percentage or a proportion-correct effect cannot be computed from the paper; only the test statistics can be cited.

reporting_issues.issue: The study is described as double-blind, but the placebo-day BPRS scores are essentially invariant (thought disorder 3.0, SD 0.0 at all three time points; hostility 3.1, SEM 0.1), and the authors state they could not run analyses of covariance with the BPRS because of the lack of variance in the placebo condition.
reporting_issues.consequence: The blind cannot have survived for the raters once a score moved, and the paper reports no blinding check; the BPRS results must be read as unblinded ratings.

reporting_issues.issue: The interval between the two test days is given only as 'at least one day', with no upper limit and no report of the actual intervals, and no period or order effect is reported.
reporting_issues.consequence: Practice effects on a repeated word-list procedure cannot be ruled out, although the within-person placebo day makes a systematic bias in favour of the drug effect unlikely.

disagreements.resolution: Accepted after reading p. 303 rendered at 150 dpi: the sentence reads 'decreases in attention from baseline at +55 minutes of the ketamine infusion', and the recall and recognition counts follow in the same run of sentences.
